plain: Amendment 81 would add a rule to Colorado's Constitution. Officials would have to notify federal immigration authorities after charging certain people whose legal status they cannot confirm. Those people are anyone charged with a violent crime, or with any crime if they have a prior felony.

short_version.text: Amendment 81 would require officials to notify federal immigration authorities when they charge someone with a violent crime, or with any crime after a prior felony, and can't confirm the person's legal status. Some sheriffs already notify ICE; state law limits others. The argument is public safety against acting on a charge before guilt is decided.

agree_means: Yes requires officers, jail staff and prosecutors to try to check legal status. They must notify the federal Department of Homeland Security within 72 hours of charging. It needs 55% of the vote.
disagree_means: No keeps current law: agencies may help with federal criminal cases but not civil immigration enforcement, and counties set their own notification practices.

stakes.text: Research is split on whether cooperating with ICE changes crime reporting. A 2024 study of the Secure Communities program found Hispanic victims reported fewer crimes. A 2021 analysis by the Center for Immigration Studies, which favors lower immigration, found immigrants report as often as the native-born.

sources.title: Immigration Enforcement and Public Safety (NBER conference paper by Gonçalves, Jácome and Weisburst)
sources.quote: we find that the program reduced the likelihood that Hispanic victims reported crimes to police and increased the victimization of Hispanics.

sources.title: Are Immigrants Less Willing to Report Crime? (Center for Immigration Studies)
sources.quote: immigrant victimizations are just as likely, and in some cases more likely, to be reported to police than crimes against the native-born.

stakes.text: Notice comes at charging, not conviction, and with a prior felony even a traffic charge counts. case_for.text: Supporters, led by Advance Colorado, say state law now blocks officers from reporting violent offenders and repeat felons. They cite a possible $50,000 fine and say Amendment 81 removes that risk.

sources.title: Immigration reporting measure fuels debate over Colorado’s role with ICE (Colorado Politics)
sources.quote: this gives Colorado law enforcement the ability to report violent criminals or repeat felons if they are here illegally without facing a $50,000 fine from the state.

case_for.text: Supporters also say one statewide rule would replace a patchwork of local policies and help remove people who may be a public-safety threat.

sources.title: 2026 Colorado State Ballot Information Booklet (Blue Book) (Colorado Legislative Council Staff)
sources.quote: The measure creates a new uniform statewide standard for cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

case_against.text: Opponents say a charge is an allegation, not guilt, and deportation should not follow before a fair trial. ACLU Colorado argues the measure violates the Constitution's due process clause.

sources.title: 2026 Colorado State Ballot Information Booklet (Blue Book) (Colorado Legislative Council Staff)
sources.quote: Criminal charges are allegations, not findings of guilt, and individuals should not face potentially life-altering immigration consequences, including deportation, before receiving a fair trial.

sources.title: Immigration reporting measure fuels debate over Colorado’s role with ICE (Colorado Politics)
sources.quote: Mendoza argued that Proposition 81 violates the Due Process Clause of the U.S. Constitution

case_against.text: Opponents, including several district attorneys, say it would erode trust. Denver DA Walsh says officers can now tell victims and witnesses they do not take part in federal civil immigration enforcement. They could not under Amendment 81.

sources.title: Immigration reporting measure fuels debate over Colorado’s role with ICE (Colorado Politics)
sources.quote: Today, state and local law enforcement in this state can truthfully tell the victims and witnesses to a crime that we do not participate in federal civil immigration enforcement

sources.title: 2026 Colorado State Ballot Information Booklet (Blue Book) (Colorado Legislative Council Staff)
sources.quote: This breakdown in trust may deter some individuals from reporting crimes, cooperating with investigations, or seeking assistance for fear of subjecting themselves or members of their community to immigration enforcement.

research_notes: Claude in Chrome was not connected, so I used the built-in Browser pane (own tab) for the Center for Immigration Studies report (curl returned 403); its quote was checked against the rendered page text afterward (matched). The NBER paper studies the Secure Communities program, not notification at charging, so it is an analogy, not a test of Amendment 81. The CIS report uses 2017-2019 national survey data. I found no Colorado-specific data on crime reporting or on how many people would be notified. I did not verify a '2023 law' (none appeared in any source read); the laws cited are HB19-1124 and SB25-276. The $50,000 fine in the Blue Book applies to sharing certain nonpublic personal information; Advance Colorado's claim that it covers reporting charges is theirs and is disputed by sheriff practice, so I framed it as disputed. Colorado Politics calls the measure 'Proposition 81' in places. Jail-cost figures beyond the fiscal note were not found. Web search budget ran out mid-session.
